newsitem.title: UK: Illness stymies Britain's first war crimes trial.
newsitem.headline: Illness stymies Britain's first war crimes trial.

text.p: Britain's first war crimes trial collapsed on Friday when a jury ruled that Szymon Serafinowicz, a former police commander in Nazi-occupied Belarus, was not mentally fit to face a full trial.
Serafinowicz, 86, was accused of being involved in the Nazi programme which wiped out the Jewish population of Byelorussia during World War Two.
The prosecution alleged he had taken part in a massacre in the town of Mir in November 1941 when up to 2,000 Jews -- a third of the town's population -- were killed.
He had also led his forces in convoys of horse-driven sledges which swept through Byelorussian villages, rounding up the Jews and kiling them, according the prosecution.
Serafinowicz denied the charges and a jury in London accepted his defence team's assertion that he was suffering from dementia, probably caused by Alzheimer's disease, and was not fit to stand trial.
"The effect of this (decision) is a permanent stay on these proceedings," prosecution lawyer Derek Spencer said. "It does not amount to a discharge or an acquittal on the merits of the case."
Friday's decision followed an eight-day pre-trial hearing, held in secret for legal reasons.

If the case had gone to trial it would have been the first held under a controversial 1991 British law. The government had to invoke special powers to introduce it after it was thrown out by the House of Lords (upper house of parliament).
Serafinowicz, who came to Britain after the war and worked as a carpenter until he was 70, is a tiny, frail-looking man with a pinched, sunken face.
He appeared to fall asleep several times during the hearing though at other times he seemed very alert, giving broad toothless smiles.
When the jury announced their decision, he appeared confused and his lawyer said he leaned over to ask him "What have they said "yes' to?"
Because he is partially deaf, Serafinowicz sat in the well of the court, rather than the dock, so that he could hear.
Witnesses said Serafinowicz had been eager to go to trial because he believed he would have been acquitted.
"I want to go ahead. I will enjoy myself, a big pleasure...I want to clear my name," one witness said Serafinowicz told him.
A psychiatrist called by the defence said that Serafinowicz was probably suffering from dementia and would not be able to follow a trial or give evidence.
An independent psychiatrist appointed by the court agreed, but the prosecution's expert witness said he believed Serafinowicz was faking his symptoms.

The prosecution said replies Serafinowicz gave in a mental test -- that a giraffe has two legs and that the season was summer on a day when it was snowing -- were so ludicrous that he had to be feigning.The defence dismissed the suggestion.
"Are you looking at the best actor this country has produced in recent times or are you looking at a sick old man, near the end of his life?" defence lawyer William Clegg asked the jury.

Serafinowicz was arrested in July 1995 by a special police war crimes unit set up after the 1991 act was passed. The unit has investigated around 350 cases, but now has only a handful left because most suspects have either died or been cleared.

Britain's Crown Prosecution Service says it is considering bringing five cases to court, but Serafinowicz's was believed to have been the one it thought most likely to succeed. His case is believed to have cost about five million pounds ($8 million). ($1=.5979 Pound)
